one_liner: Rust reimplementation of GNU coreutils; release notes claim faster sort, base64, expand and nl than GNU, without a published harness.
what_it_does: uutils coreutils reimplements every GNU coreutils program in Rust as one multicall `coreutils` binary (or separate binaries), aiming at byte-identical output and exit codes, with differences from GNU treated as bugs. It is a command-line drop-in rather than a library, runs on Linux, macOS, the BSDs, Windows and WASI, and has shipped as the default coreutils on Ubuntu since 25.10. Each utility is also a uu_* crate exposing a uumain entry point.
how_it_is_fast: sort runs its in-memory sort on rayon (par_sort_unstable_by, or par_sort_by for -s and -u) with a thread pool sized from --parallel or std::thread::available_parallelism, parses -n keys once per line, and in UTF-8 locales computes an ICU4X collation sort key once per line (compute_sort_key_utf8, Shifted and Quaternary to mimic GNU) so comparisons are plain byte compares. base64 uses the base64-simd crate (switched in PR #8578, September 2025). expand writes buffers with no tab, backspace or carriage return straight through, without per-character processing. Since August 2026 the release binaries are built with PGO trained on exactly the claimed utilities (util/build-pgo.sh); docs/src/performance.md credits PGO with -17% on sort and -22% to -29% on nl, fold and uniq -c.
when_to_use: Scripts that must behave the same on Linux, macOS, Windows and WASI with GNU-style options.
Large in-memory sort jobs on many-core machines, plain whole-line keys, release or PGO build: an outside user measured 100.2 ms against GNU's 152.4 ms on /usr/share/dict/words (issue #13193).
Bulk base64 encoding or decoding of large files on SIMD-capable CPUs, where base64-simd does the work.
Systems that already ship it by default (Ubuntu 25.10 and later), where checking the GNU-relative claims for your own workload is cheap with the hyperfine recipe in docs/src/performance.md.
when_not_to_use: sort -m on already sorted input or sort -z: the same outside run measured GNU 7.66x and 13.72x faster (issue #13193, closed with no fix recorded).

Pipelines that depend on glibc's exact collation order in UTF-8 locales: uutils collates with ICU4X, and an April 2026 guide warns of divergence under en_US.UTF-8 (search snippet only); use LC_ALL=C for both.
Scripts that exercise rare GNU options or edge cases: release 0.12.0 still fails 21 GNU tests (653 pass).
Utilities with open slower-than-GNU issues: date (#14750), factor (#11439, 'extremely slower'), mktemp (#11064), echo (#10852), cat (#10832) and true startup (#11340).
Debug builds, which ran 10x slower than GNU sort in issue #13193 and about 48x slower in issue #11258.

integration.form: crate (multicall CLI binary `coreutils`; per-utility uu_* crates with a uumain entry point)
integration.dependencies: sort: rayon, memchr, foldhash, bigdecimal, ICU4X (icu_collator, icu_decimal, icu_datetime) through uucore; base64: base64-simd and data-encoding through uucore; optional OpenSSL libcrypto for the checksum utilities (feature openssl); libselinux and libclang only for SELinux tools.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.88.0 (workspace rust-version); tested against stable, beta and nightly.
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, FreeBSD and other BSDs, Windows, WASI (sort runs single-threaded on WASI); musl and glibc release binaries.
integration.thread_safety: Not applicable (command-line processes); sort uses a global rayon pool sized by --parallel, defaulting to all available cores.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — designed as a GNU coreutils drop-in and default on Ubuntu since 25.10, but 21 GNU tests still fail in 0.12.0 and UTF-8 collation comes from ICU4X, not glibc

gotchas: No harness behind the numbers: the 0.3.0 'Compared to GNU' list (sort 3.72x and 1.46x, expand 1.80x, nl 1.57x, unexpand 1.50x, base64 1.20x, fold 1.19x, uniq -c 1.13x) and the 0.11.0 join 2.5x give no hardware, input, locale, thread count or GNU version, and the in-tree Divan and CodSpeed benches time uutils against itself. The same 0.3.0 changelog says 'fold: improve the performances - now same as GNU', which contradicts the 1.19x line.

Unequal settings are easy to hit: uutils sort uses every available core unless --parallel is given, collates UTF-8 locales with precomputed ICU4X keys while C and C.UTF-8 use byte comparison, and shipped binaries since August 2026 are PGO-trained on sort, sort -n, nl, fold, expand, unexpand, uniq -c, join and base64. expand copies tab-free buffers straight through, so a tab-free test file measures a copy loop. Pin LC_ALL, --parallel and the build type before comparing.

Pathological regressions have appeared after release-note speedups: issue #11258 measured `sort` of about 100 million random integers under en_US.UTF-8 at 51m38s against GNU's 1m47s (about 29x slower); it was closed by PR #11412, though the reporter was not sure it was fixed. In issue #8574, base64 0.1.0 was 7.9x slower than GNU on 4 GB files (19.556 s vs 2.461 s, i7-13620H) before the base64-simd switch.

Issue #9213 (still open) reports base64 --decode reading all of stdin first (about 325 MB peak against GNU's 1 MB on a 500 MB stream); current src/uu/base32/src/base_common.rs streams every format except Base58, so this looks fixed in code even though the issue is open.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick uutils when you want the whole GNU-compatible tool set, the same across platforms; single-purpose siblings such as hck or tuc (cut), huniq or runiq (sort | uniq), cw or wz (wc) and rust-sort are faster at their one job but change the interface or semantics. RustyBox is the other multi-tool Rust userland in the catalog, but uutils targets GNU option compatibility and is the one Ubuntu ships.
verified_claims_summary: The only GNU-relative figures are first-party release-note highlights: 0.3.0 (24 October, year not shown, released when the GNU test reference moved to coreutils 9.8) claims sort 3.72x faster for default sorting and 1.46x for numeric, expand 1.80x, nl 1.57x, unexpand 1.50x, base64 1.20x, fold 1.19x and uniq -c 1.13x, and 0.11.0 (31 August 2026) claims join 2.5x; no hardware, inputs, locale, thread count, GNU version or build flags are given. Outside spot checks in the issue tracker are mixed: plain release sort on /usr/share/dict/words was 1.5x faster than GNU, while sort -m and -z were 7.7x and 13.7x slower.
status_note: Very active (last commit 2026-10-11, release 0.12.0 on 17 September 2026, 24.2k stars), MIT-licensed and the Ubuntu default since 25.10; treat the speedups as unreproduced first-party claims and benchmark your own workload with LC_ALL, --parallel and the build type pinned.
